el-0: After a Broken Wrist: Exercises and Recovery After the Cast Comes Off | İhsan Eren
el-1: Cast off, but your wrist is stiff and weak? What to expect after a broken wrist, when it gets back to normal, and whether you need physiotherapy. Warning signs and six exercises to do at home.
el-3: Your cast is off, but your wrist is stiff, your hand weak and a little swollen? This is very normal. A broken wrist usually heals in 6–12 weeks; after the cast comes off, movement and strength return with regular exercise and gradually using your hand for daily tasks. Starting to use your hand, even if you feel apprehensive, is the most important step in recovery.

el-22: Six exercises to free up the wrist
el-23: Start with about 10 repetitions of each movement, in short sessions 3–4 times a day. As it gets easier, increase the number of repetitions and the range of movement. Mild pain is normal; if the pain becomes severe or continuous, see your doctor.
el-24: Rest your forearm on a table with your hand over the edge. Let your wrist drop down as far as it can, then lift it up. As pain allows, you can help gently with your other hand.
el-26: Hold your arm out in front with the elbow straight and the palm facing up. With your other hand, gently pull your fingers down and back until you feel a stretch on the inside of your wrist and forearm. Push as far as pain allows.
el-27: 10 reps or 15–20 seconds, 3–4 times a day
el-28: Keep your elbow bent and close to your body. Turn your palm to face up, then down. Try not to let your elbow move away from your body.
el-29: Making a fist and opening the hand
el-30: Make a tight fist, then spread your fingers as wide as you can.
el-32: Move your thumb towards the base of your little finger, then stretch it out as far as you can. Increase the movement as pain allows.
el-33: Hold a soft ball and squeeze it, hold for a few seconds and let go. As it becomes more comfortable, squeeze harder or use a firmer ball.
el-34: My cast is off but my wrist is still very stiff. Is that normal?
el-35: Yes. After weeks in a cast, it is expected that the wrist and fingers are stiff and the muscles weak. Some pain and swelling is also normal, especially when you start using your hand again. These ease steadily with time and use. The biggest improvement usually comes in the first 1–2 months, but some swelling and stiffness can last several months.
el-36: Do I have to have physiotherapy?
el-37: Not everyone does. A Cochrane review of 26 studies found no clear difference between a home exercise programme taught by a therapist and the same programme plus regular physiotherapy; but the quality of the evidence is low. If stiffness or pain is improving more slowly than expected, support from a physiotherapist can be helpful.
el-38: What is complex regional pain syndrome?
el-39: It is pain that can rarely develop after a fracture, out of proportion to the injury and often burning. It may come with very sensitive skin, swelling, changes in colour and temperature, sweating and stiffness. Using your hand as normally as possible and doing the recommended exercises may help reduce the risk. If you notice these signs, you can see your doctor or physiotherapist early.
el-40: When can I drive and lift heavy things?
el-41: It is recommended not to drive or lift heavy things until your doctor says it is safe. You can use your hand for daily tasks gradually, more as it becomes comfortable; but doing too much exercise at once can increase the pain.
el-42: Fractures after a fall can be related to bone health: you can look at the osteoporosis and falls prevention guides.
